It says her origins are unknown, and that the earliest known appearance is an anonymous ghost story posted on 26 August 2008.

sources.title: Hasshaku-sama
sources.supports: The eight-foot woman, the death curse in the countryside, and the 26 August 2008 anonymous post as the earliest known text.

parodyPotential: A tower woman who is exactly too tall for the doorway and who considers that a personal curse on the architecture.

sensitivity.guidance: This is a recent anonymous story, not old folklore and not shown to be public domain. Do not copy the 2008 text or later illustrations. A very tall rural stranger is a pattern already covered with more caution under Slender Man; prefer a clearly comic height gag if used at all.

name: La Llorona
origin: Hispanic American folklore, especially Mexico and the southwestern United States
facts: La Llorona ('the Weeping Woman') is a vengeful ghost in Hispanic American folklore. She is said to roam near water mourning children she drowned in a river. Hearing her cry is said to bring misfortune, death, or a ruined life.
The article says the lore is well known in Mexico and the southwestern United States and is told through Mexico, Central America, and northern South America.

sources.title: La Llorona
sources.supports: The weeping ghost by water, the drowned children, and the misfortune that follows her cry.

parodyPotential: Not as a child-death joke. A tower ghost who weeps because a fountain was installed wrong is the furthest safe bend.

sensitivity.guidance: Do not comedy the drowning of children. The legend is living folklore across many countries. A weeping omen near water can be used only if the children are not the joke and not depicted. Specific films are copyrighted.

name: Spring-heeled Jack
origin: Victorian English urban legend, first claimed sightings 1837
facts: Spring-heeled Jack is a figure in Victorian English folklore. The article dates the first claimed sighting to 1837, with later reports across the United Kingdom, especially suburban London, the Midlands, and Scotland.

He was famous for a bizarre appearance and extraordinary leaps, and became the subject of fiction. The article says some accounts gave him sharp metallic claws, and at least two people claimed he could speak in a comprehensible way.

sources.title: Spring-heeled Jack
sources.supports: The 1837 start, the leaping stranger, the metallic claws in some accounts, and the leap into period fiction.

parodyPotential: A tower phantom whose entire combat plan is arriving from a floor he should not be able to reach.

sensitivity.guidance: The Victorian legend is old enough to treat as folklore. Some original reports describe attacks on women; do not replay those attacks. The leap and the impossible entrance are the pattern. Later comics that use the name may have their own copyrights.

name: Jersey Devil
origin: South Jersey and Philadelphia folklore
facts: The Jersey Devil, also called the Leeds Devil, is a legendary creature said to live in the forests of the New Jersey Pine Barrens. It is often described as a flying biped with hooves, with many variations.
A common description in the article is a kangaroo-like or wyvern-like biped with a horse- or goat-like head, leathery bat-like wings, horns, small clawed arms, cloven hooves, and a forked tail.

sources.title: Jersey Devil
sources.supports: The Pine Barrens cryptid, the Leeds Devil alias, and the winged hoofed biped description.

parodyPotential: A tower mascot assembled from spare animal parts that cannot agree which end is the front.

sensitivity.guidance: Folklore. The Leeds family birth-curse versions can be ugly about a real surname; prefer the composite creature over a joke about a named family. Sports-team logos are trademarks.

name: The Backrooms
origin: Anonymous 4chan post, 2019, using a 2002 photograph
facts: The Backrooms are a fictional location from a 2019 4chan thread. They are usually shown as an impossibly large extradimensional complex of empty rooms, entered by leaving reality. The article calls them a well-known liminal-space and creepypasta example.

The concept began as an anonymous caption of a photo of a large empty room with a yellow cast. The photo was taken in 2002 in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, in a former furniture store. The caption warns that if you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas you end up in the Backrooms. Later works include a found-footage series by Kane Pixels.

sources.title: The Backrooms
sources.supports: The 2019 4chan origin, the yellow empty rooms, the 2002 photo, the noclip caption, and the later Kane Pixels series.

parodyPotential: A tower floor that is only carpet, humming lights, and a map that apologizes for not existing.

sensitivity.guidance: The anonymous 2019 caption is not a license to copy later Backrooms monsters, levels, or Kane Pixels' footage. Those are copyrighted. An endless bland interior you enter by a wrong exit is the pattern.

name: Candle Cove
origin: Creepypasta by Kris Straub, published 2009 on Ichor Falls
facts: Candle Cove is an online horror story by cartoonist Kris Straub. It is a forum discussion about a fictional children's television show. Straub has said he was inspired by an Onion article about an adult still having nightmares about the 1970s show Lidsville.
The article says Straub published the story in 2009 on ichorfalls.com under a Creative Commons license, as part of his horror stories about the fictional town of Ichor Falls.

sources.title: Candle Cove
sources.supports: Straub's authorship, the fake-children's-show frame, the 2009 publication, and the Creative Commons release.

parodyPotential: A tower channel that only some of the party remember, and that insists it was always on the schedule.

sensitivity.guidance: Creative Commons is not public domain and is not permission to paste the story into a commercial game. Do not copy Straub's text, the puppet, or the show's name. A half-remembered cursed broadcast is the pattern.

name: Siren Head
origin: Creature by Trevor Henderson, 2018
facts: The creepypasta list says Siren Head was created in 2018 by Canadian horror illustrator Trevor Henderson. It is a 40-foot-tall, thin, skeletal figure with rotting emaciated skin and two rusted siren-like megaphones for a head.

The sirens sometimes blare random words in a staticky voice. In other stories they scream garbled music, radio reports, people calling for help, or Emergency Alert System broadcasts, mimicking sounds to lure people into the forest. The article says it became widely popular online in 2020.

sources.title: List of creepypastas
sources.supports: The Siren Head section: Henderson, 2018, the megaphone head, the lure-by-mimicry, and the 2020 popularity.

parodyPotential: A tower pole that is mostly loudspeaker, and that lures people by playing the wrong floor's battle music.

sensitivity.guidance: Siren Head's name and the siren-megaphone design belong to Trevor Henderson. Do not copy them. A tall thing that mimics a helpful sound is a much older pattern and must look like something else.

name: SCP Foundation
origin: Collaborative fiction wiki, moved to Wikidot in July 2008
facts: The SCP Foundation is a fictional secret organization and the premise of a collaborative wiki. It captures, contains, and studies paranormal anomalies called SCPs, while hiding them from the public. The article describes the project as horror, science fiction, and urban fantasy, mostly written as case files.

It says that when the wiki moved to Wikidot in July 2008, new Wikidot wikis defaulted to CC BY-SA 3.0, and the staff therefore accidentally adopted that license. It also says the original SCP-173 text was placed in Creative Commons by its author in 2013 because earlier license status was uncertain.

sources.title: SCP Foundation
sources.supports: The containment organization, the case-file format, and the accidental CC BY-SA 3.0 adoption plus the later SCP-173 release.

parodyPotential: A tower archive that files monsters by how inconvenient they are, and that is more afraid of a missing label than of the monster.

sensitivity.guidance: CC BY-SA is not public domain. Share-alike text cannot be pasted into a closed game. Do not copy SCP numbers, procedures, or creature designs. A bureau that contains oddities in files is the pattern.

name: Elizabeth Báthory
origin: Hungarian history, 1560–1614, and later folklore
facts: Elizabeth Báthory (7 August 1560 – 21 August 1614) was a Hungarian noblewoman and alleged serial killer. The article says she was imprisoned in Csejte Castle (now Čachtice, Slovakia) until she died in her sleep in 1614.

Legends of vampiric habits, including the tale that she bathed in the blood of virgins to stay young, are described as rumours written down as if factual more than a century after her death. The article says at least three later historians repeated them, and that modern historians consider those stories unreliable.

sources.title: Elizabeth Báthory
sources.supports: The historical imprisonment and death, and the article's statement that the blood-bath legend is a late, unreliable rumour.

parodyPotential: Not recommended. A vain immortal who moisturizes with something harmless is a different joke and should not use her name.

sensitivity.guidance: She was a real person accused of killing real people. Do not comedy the accusations, the victims, or the blood-bath rumour. The research point is that the vampire story was written long after her death and is considered unreliable. Do not use her as a boss.

name: Mary I of England
origin: Tudor history; the nickname Bloody Mary
facts: Mary I was the only surviving child of Henry VIII and his first wife, Catherine of Aragon. The article says she was expected to reverse the Protestant reforms of the previous reign.

During her five-year reign, more than 280 religious dissenters were burned at the stake in the Marian persecutions. The article says later commentators labeled her Bloody Mary because of those executions.

sources.title: Mary I
sources.supports: The Tudor queen, the Marian burnings of more than 280 dissenters, and the later nickname Bloody Mary.

parodyPotential: Do not parody the executions. The nickname is only here so it is not confused with the mirror folklore in INS-05-027.

sensitivity.guidance: The burnings were real. Do not make a boss out of them or out of Mary I. The mirror Bloody Mary is a separate, unsettled folklore record and is not proven to be this queen.

name: Zheng Yi Sao
origin: South China Sea piracy, 1801–1810
facts: Zheng Yi Sao, also known in the West as Ching Shih, was a Chinese pirate leader in the South China Sea from 1801 to 1810. The article says she was born Shi Yang in 1775 and married the pirate Zheng Yi.
Under the fleet she came to command, by 1805 there were about 400 junks and between 40,000 and 70,000 pirates. The article presents her as the leader of that confederation.

sources.title: Zheng Yi Sao
sources.supports: The historical pirate leader, the 1801–1810 dates, and the scale of about 400 junks and tens of thousands of pirates.

parodyPotential: A tower admiral whose fleet is so large the battle is mostly roll call.

sensitivity.guidance: Historical commander, not a copyrighted character. Do not invent a sexualized origin. The usable pattern is a pirate boss whose power is the size of the fleet and the code that holds it, not a costume from a film.

name: Anne Bonny
origin: Golden Age of Piracy; early biography in Captain Charles Johnson, 1724
facts: Anne Bonny (likely died December 1733) was a pirate who served under John Rackham. The article calls her one of the few recorded women pirates of the Golden Age and one of the best known.

It says much of her background is unknown, and that the first biography is Captain Charles Johnson's 1724 A General History of the Pyrates. Johnson says she was born in Ireland, the illegitimate daughter of an attorney and his servant.

sources.title: Anne Bonny
sources.supports: Service under Rackham, the scarcity of records, and Johnson's 1724 book as the first biography.

parodyPotential: A tower corsair whose legend is mostly one book, and who keeps correcting the footnotes mid-fight.

sensitivity.guidance: Johnson's 1724 book mixes report and storytelling. Do not treat every colorful detail as settled fact. She is not a fantasy character to costume from a recent TV series; those costumes are copyrighted.

name: Davy Jones's locker
origin: Sailors' euphemism, in print by 1726
facts: Davy Jones's locker is the traditional resting place of drowned sailors and travellers. The article calls it a euphemism for drowning or shipwreck, the remains consigned to the bottom of the sea, and says the phrase is first used in print in 1726.
The article quotes a definition of David Jones as the devil, the spirit of the sea, compared with northern spirits such as the Necken or Draugr.

sources.title: Davy Jones's locker
sources.supports: The drowned-sailors' resting place, the 1726 print date, and the devil-of-the-sea definition.

parodyPotential: A tower purser who keeps a locker for anything that fell overboard, including arguments.

sensitivity.guidance: The locker and the old sea-devil name are sailors' lore. The tentacled captain from Pirates of the Caribbean is a separate copyrighted design. Do not draw that character.

name: Faust and Mephistopheles
origin: German legend of a scholar's pact, later Goethe and many retellings
facts: Faust is the legend of a scholar who makes a pact at a crossroads, trading his soul for unlimited knowledge and worldly pleasure. The article says related devil-pact tales include the early Dutch play Mariken van Nieumeghen.

Mephistopheles is the devil's representative in the legend. Faust knowingly trades his soul, condemning himself to Hell, for what Mephistopheles offers. The article calls Mephistopheles a stock character who began as the chief devil of this legend and spread into later art.

sources.title: Faust
sources.supports: The crossroads pact of soul for knowledge and pleasure.

sources.title: Mephistopheles
sources.supports: Mephistopheles as the devil's agent in the Faust legend and as a later stock character.

parodyPotential: A tower clerk who will sign anything if the other party initials the price, and who is very clear about the price.

sensitivity.guidance: The legend is old. Goethe's specific lines, if quoted at length, and modern film devils are not free to paste. A signed bargain with a visible price is the pattern. Do not copy a studio's demon design.

name: Headless Horseman
origin: European headless-rider folklore and Washington Irving, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow (1820)
facts: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow is an 1820 short story by Washington Irving, written while he was living abroad and printed in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. It is the famous American telling of a headless horseman.

The Headless Horseman article says that, depending on the legend, the rider is carrying his head or searching for it. It notes a local story of a Hessian soldier decapitated by a cannonball, and also says there is no documented record of that body being found and buried. It adds that Irving likely knew older European folklore of a headless rider, attested since the Middle Ages.

sources.title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow
sources.supports: Irving's 1820 story as the famous American version.

sources.title: Headless Horseman
sources.supports: The carrying-or-seeking head, the undocumented Hessian burial claim, and older European headless riders.

parodyPotential: A tower courier who cannot file a report because he has misplaced the head that holds the face everyone recognizes.

sensitivity.guidance: Irving's 1820 story and the older rider folklore are the public layer. This record does not certify a legal public-domain opinion beyond the 1820 date and the folklore. Disney and later film horsemen are protected designs. Do not copy them.

name: Pied Piper of Hamelin
origin: German legend of Hamelin, medieval, with a 1284 town memory
facts: In the familiar legend, the town hires a piper to lure rats away with his music. When the citizens refuse to pay, he uses the same power on their children and leads them away. The article says this version spread as folklore and appears in Goethe and the Brothers Grimm.

It also quotes a Hamelin record dated 1284, on the feast of Saints John and Paul, about a well-dressed young man of about thirty who entered by the West Gate and then began to play. The article presents that inscription as part of the town's memory of children being lost.

sources.title: Pied Piper of Hamelin
sources.supports: The unpaid rat-catcher who leads the children away, and the 1284 Hamelin record of a strikingly dressed young man.

parodyPotential: A tower exterminator who clears the rats, is not paid, and then leads the paperwork out of the building.

sensitivity.guidance: Do not comedy the children being taken. The safe door is the unpaid contractor and the rats. The music that moves a crowd is the pattern. Do not depict harm to children.

name: Vanishing hitchhiker
origin: International urban legend, classified by folklorists
facts: The vanishing hitchhiker, also called the ghostly or phantom hitchhiker, is an urban legend in which a ghost asks for a ride. A common form summarized in the article: a young woman's ghost asks for a ride, then disappears from the closed car without the driver noticing, after giving an address.
In many tellings she leaves a token, often the overcoat she borrowed, on her grave, which corroborates the ride.

sources.title: Vanishing hitchhiker
sources.supports: The ghost passenger who vanishes from a closed car, and the borrowed coat left on a grave.

parodyPotential: A tower passenger who vanishes between floors and leaves a borrowed scarf on a memorial plaque.

sensitivity.guidance: A widespread folklore type, not one studio's character. Do not pin the joke on a real traffic death. The vanish-and-leave-proof structure is the pattern.

name: The Hook
origin: American urban legend, in circulation by the mid-1950s, printed by Dear Abby in 1960
facts: The Hook, or the Hookman, is an American urban legend about a killer with a hook for a hand attacking a couple in a parked car. Many versions describe a faceless old man in a raincoat and rain hat.
The article says the story is thought to date from at least the mid-1950s and gained attention when Dear Abby reprinted it in 1960. It calls the tale a morality archetype in later popular culture.

sources.title: The Hook
sources.supports: The hook-handed attacker, the parked-car setting, the raincoat silhouette, and the 1960 Dear Abby printing.

parodyPotential: A tower usher with a coat hook for a hand who is mostly a problem for unattended coats.

sensitivity.guidance: Folklore, not a film slasher. Do not stage an attack on a couple as the joke. A hook silhouette and a scare that turns out to be a hanging coat are enough.

name: Pope Lick Monster
origin: Louisville, Kentucky urban legend, tied to a real railroad trestle
facts: The Pope Lick Monster, often called the Goat Man, is a part-man, part-goat, part-sheep creature said to live beneath a railroad trestle over Pope Lick Creek in the Fisherville area of Louisville, Kentucky. Stories disagree about its origin and how it takes victims. Some say it uses hypnosis or voice mimicry to lure people onto the trestle, where a train kills them.
The article has a deaths section: several people have died on or near the trestle while pursuing the legend, including a 17-year-old struck and killed by a train in 1988.

sources.title: Pope Lick Monster
sources.supports: The goat-like creature under the trestle, the lure stories, and the documented real deaths of people seeking the legend.

parodyPotential: Not on a real bridge and not as a dare. A tower goat that lives under a staircase is a different creature.

sensitivity.guidance: People have died on this real trestle, including a teenager in 1988. Do not name the victims in game text, do not describe how to reach the bridge, and do not make a challenge out of visiting it. Do not use this legend as a boss.

name: Captain William Kidd
origin: Scottish privateer, hanged 1701; later treasure legend
facts: William Kidd (about 1645 – 23 May 1701), also Captain Kidd, was a Scottish privateer. The article says he was likely born in Dundee and later lived in New York, and that by 1695 he held a royal commission connected to the Earl of Bellomont.

He was found guilty and hanged in 1701. After his death he was romanticized in fiction. The article says the belief that he had left buried treasure did a great deal to build the legend and inspired treasure hunts for centuries.

sources.title: William Kidd
sources.supports: The privateer's career, the 1701 hanging, and the buried-treasure belief as the engine of the later legend.

parodyPotential: A tower privateer whose map leads only to another map, and who is more famous for the hole than for the gold.

sensitivity.guidance: Historical figure. The hanging is not a joke. The usable pattern is a treasure legend that outgrew the person, and a map that may be the whole monster.

name: Jaeger and Kaiju (Pacific Rim)
origin: Pacific Rim (2013 film), directed by Guillermo del Toro
facts: Pacific Rim is a 2013 film set in a future war against the Kaiju, colossal sea monsters that come through an interdimensional portal on the Pacific Ocean floor.
Humanity answers with Jaegers, gigantic humanoid machines. Each is controlled by two co-pilots whose minds are joined by a mental link the film calls the Drift.

sources.title: Pacific Rim (film)
sources.supports: Ocean kaiju from a portal, and two-pilot Jaegers linked by the Drift.

parodyPotential: A tower machine that needs two pilots who agree, and that spends the first phase on the argument.

sensitivity.guidance: Jaeger, Kaiju as used in this film, the Drift, and the category system (not described in the fetched lead, so not recorded) are protected. Two people sharing one giant machine is the pattern.
